content.text:
<instructions>
Generate a single self-contained HTML file that runs directly in a browser.

Build a photoreal, full-3D lava lamp. A classic tapered lava lamp stands on a surface in a dim room. Inside the glass, a bulb heats colored wax suspended in a tinted liquid. Wax blobs swell at the bottom, detach, rise, stretch, merge, split, cool near the top, and sink back down. It must feel like a real object you could stare at for minutes, not a looping animation or a flat 2D effect.
</instructions>

<core-experience>
The page is one fullscreen 3D scene centered on the lamp.

- The lamp is the hero. It is lit, running, and visibly moving on first load. Do not require a click before the wax moves.
- The user can orbit around the lamp, zoom within sensible limits, and see it from any side. The motion and lighting must hold up from every angle, including close-up.
- The lamp is the main light source of the scene. Its glow spills onto the surface it stands on and the nearby room, and that light flickers and shifts as wax passes in front of the bulb.
- Wax motion is continuous and never visibly repeats. Blobs vary in size, speed, and shape over time.

The result should feel like a premium product shot of a real lava lamp, filmed at night.
</core-experience>

<lamp-object>
Model a recognizable lava lamp, not a capsule or a cylinder.

- A tapered glass vessel, wider at the bottom, with real thickness, a rounded top, and a sealed bottom.
- A conical metal base that hides the bulb, and a matching metal cap. Brushed or polished metal with visible reflections.
- A visible power cord leading off the surface, and a small physical switch on the base or cord.
- Proportions and scale must read as a real tabletop object.
</lamp-object>

<wax-and-liquid>
The wax is the core of the experience.

- The wax is a continuous, merging fluid volume. Blobs must smoothly fuse when they touch and neck apart when they separate. Separate spheres that overlap or pop are not acceptable.
- Motion is driven by a heat model: wax near the bulb warms, expands, and rises; wax near the cap cools, contracts, and sinks. A pool of warm wax stays at the bottom and feeds new blobs.
- Rising blobs stretch vertically and wobble. Small droplets can pinch off from larger ones. Falling blobs are slower and denser looking.
- Blobs stay inside the glass. They follow the taper of the vessel and never clip through the walls, cap, or base.
- The wax looks translucent and warm, brighter where it is thin and near the bulb, darker and more saturated where it is thick. A subsurface-scattering look is expected.
- The liquid is tinted, slightly hazy, and refracts what is behind it. The wax color and liquid color must contrast.
</wax-and-liquid>

<controls>
Provide a small, elegant control panel that does not cover the lamp.

- Power switch. Turning the lamp off fades the bulb and the room light, and the wax gradually slows, cools, and settles into a pool at the bottom. Turning it back on warms the wax first; the first blob takes a few seconds to form and rise, like a real lamp.
- At least four color presets that change both the wax and the liquid, including a classic red wax in yellow liquid.
- Heat or flow speed.
- Wax amount.
- Optional: room light level, slow motion, an auto-orbit camera.

Every control must visibly change the scene in real time.
</controls>

<rendering>
Push the rendering as far as a single HTML file allows while staying smooth.

- Three.js, loaded from a pinned CDN version. three/addons from that same version are allowed.
- The wax may be rendered with raymarched signed distance fields, marching cubes, or any technique that produces a smooth merging surface. It must be properly composited with the glass and the scene.
- Physically based glass: refraction or transmission, Fresnel reflections, visible thickness, and specular highlights from the room.
- Physically based metal on the base and cap with environment reflections. Generate the environment in code or with Three.js RoomEnvironment. Do not depend on an external HDR file.
- The wax and the bulb glow. Use bloom or an equivalent so the glow reads as light, not as a flat color.
- The lamp casts light and soft shadows onto the surface. The surface itself has a believable material such as wood, stone, or fabric.
- Tone mapping (ACES or filmic) is required. Subtle film grain, vignette, or depth of field are allowed if they improve the shot.
- A dim but readable room: a table or shelf surface, a wall, and a few simple props are enough to give scale and catch the light.
</rendering>

<performance>
The page must stay smooth on a modern laptop.

- Target a stable high frame rate at full-window resolution. Use a resolution scale or adaptive quality for expensive passes if needed.
- Keep raymarch step counts, blob counts, and post passes bounded.
- Advance the wax simulation with a fixed timestep so a frame hitch cannot make blobs explode or escape the glass.
</performance>

<output-format>
One HTML file only. No extra JS, CSS, images, models, or texture files. No package manager and no dev server. Three.js may load from a CDN. Everything else, including shaders and procedural textures, is inline.

The file must start with `<!DOCTYPE html>` and end with `</html>`.
</output-format>

<important>
- You MUST write the result directly into a file named "index.html" in the current working directory.
- The page `<title>` must be your model name.
- The only visible title or brand in the page must also be your model name. Add nothing else to either title.
- Do not ask clarifying questions. Make the design and engineering decisions yourself.
</important>

Work only inside the current working directory. Do not read, list, search, or edit files outside the current working directory. Treat it as a standalone project root.

Use pnpm exclusively if dependency installation or package scripts are needed. Do not use npm.
Set the browser title and the primary visible title to your model name, using only identity information already available to you. Add nothing else to either title.
Run the relevant checks yourself. Do not edit files outside the current working directory.

## Default: Chrome Dev (one shared, signed-in Chrome)

Always run against **Chrome Dev**, Melvyn's single persistent Chrome (profile `~/.chrome-dev-profile`, CDP port 9333) where he is signed in to his accounts:

```bash
chrome-dev start   # idempotent: launches it if needed, prints http://127.0.0.1:9333
dev-browser --connect http://127.0.0.1:9333 <<'EOF'
const page = await browser.getPage("main");
EOF
```

- Need a clean logged-out session? Use `--headless`, or `DEV_BROWSER_ISOLATED=1 dev-browser --browser <name>`, and say so.
- Use descriptive page names per task (`browser.getPage("lumail-checkout")`) so parallel agents do not fight over the same tab. Close pages you no longer need with `browser.closePage(name)`. Never close Melvyn's own tabs.
- If a site asks for login in Chrome Dev, stop and ask Melvyn to sign in there (it persists). Never type passwords.
- Enforced: `dev-browser` is a shim (`~/cc/scripts/chrome-dev/dev-browser-wrapper`) that auto-starts Chrome Dev and adds `--connect http://127.0.0.1:9333` to every run, even with `--browser <name>`. It passes through untouched only with `--connect <url>`, `--headless`, or `DEV_BROWSER_ISOLATED=1` (headed throwaway Chromium, e.g. WebGL capture or HTML-to-image rendering that must not pop tabs in Chrome Dev). Never launch Chrome for Testing for normal browsing.
- `chrome-dev status|stop` to inspect or quit it. Melvyn can also open it from Spotlight: "Chrome Dev".

Never use Cursor IDE Browser MCP (`cursor-ide-browser`, `browser_navigate`, `browser_snapshot`, `browser_lock`, `browser_click`, `browser_cdp`, or any `browser_*` tool).

If `dev-browser` is missing: obey the repo's package-manager rules (no `npm install -g` when npm is forbidden). In Codex, prefer the bundled Node/Playwright/Chromium runtime for page-load, screenshot, console, and interaction checks. Install the CLI only when npm is allowed and the task needs persistence or CDP the bundled runtime cannot provide: `npm install -g dev-browser && dev-browser install`. When falling back to Playwright, keep the same proof (URL, title, errors, screenshots, exact steps) and state that the CLI was unavailable.

Write one-thing scripts. Reuse named pages (`browser.getPage("main")`) across runs. End each script by logging JSON state. Commands, flags, Page methods, locators, screenshots, forms, and CDP connect: [api-reference.md](references/api-reference.md). Open that file before inventing a Page method.

File I/O is only `~/.dev-browser/tmp/`. Never pass absolute paths to `saveScreenshot` or `writeFile`; copy out from the returned tmp path.

Helium is not auto-discovered. Launch it with `--remote-debugging-port` and connect with `dev-browser --browser helium --connect http://127.0.0.1:<port>`. An already-running Helium without CDP cannot be attached; if it must not restart, use AppleScript or Computer Use.

On script failure, the page stays put. Reconnect, screenshot, log URL/title, then continue.

I've built the lava lamp as a single `index.html`. In a real Chrome window at 1440×900 it ran at about 115 fps with no console errors, and the page title is "Claude Opus 5.5".

I checked it by taking screenshots in a real browser: on at load, switched off and back on, a colour preset change, a close-up from behind, and 20 seconds at maximum heat and flow. The cord-switch click was the only control I didn't exercise, and I can't vouch for performance on a weaker laptop beyond the automatic resolution scaling described below.

**How the wax works**
- **Shape:** the wax is drawn by raymarching a smoothly merged blend of up to 12 stretchable blobs plus a bottom pool, so blobs fuse and neck apart instead of overlapping. The wax is always clipped to the glass's inner shape, so it can't pass through the walls.
- **Heat model:** this runs on the CPU at a fixed 60 steps per second, with at most 10 steps per frame, so a frame hitch can't make blobs jump.
  - Liquid is hot near the bulb and cool near the cap. Big blobs hold heat longer.
  - Warm wax floats and cold wax sinks. Cold wax is more viscous, so falling blobs move more slowly.
- **Blob life cycle:**
  - Blobs swell out of the warm pool and stretch and wobble as they rise.
  - Small droplets sometimes pinch off the bottom of a rising blob, and big blobs occasionally split.
  - Touching blobs merge gradually and keep their combined volume. Cold wax that lands on the pool sinks back into it.
  - Merging stops once a blob reaches a size limit. Without that, the max-heat test fused everything into one giant blob.
- **Never repeats:** blobs are spawned at random and drift on wave patterns with unrelated frequencies. The lamp also pre-runs 55 seconds of simulation, so it's already going on first load.
- **Power:** off fades the bulb, the room light and the light leak at the collar, and the wax slows, cools and settles into the pool. On heats the pool first, so the first blob takes a few seconds to form and rise.

**Rendering**
- **Liquid and glass:** the room is rendered once without the lamp's interior, and the liquid shader bends rays in and out of the tapered vessel to look up the room behind it. The liquid is tinted by depth and glows from bulb light scattering in it.
- **Wax look:** it's lit by the bulb, with light dimmed where other wax sits between the surface and the bulb. Thin edges glow brighter, thick parts are darker and more saturated, and hot wax gives off a little glow of its own.
- **Glass surface:** reflections strengthen at glancing angles, the edges darken to show thickness, and there's a broad vertical highlight from a softbox placed in a room environment generated in code.
- **Room light:** the lamp's light comes from a shadow-casting light inside the glass. Its colour comes from the liquid and wax, and it dims and shifts when wax passes over the bulb.
- **Post-processing:** bloom, ACES tone mapping, film grain and a vignette. Resolution scales automatically between 0.6× and 2× the screen's pixel density to hold the frame rate.

**Scene and controls**
- **Lamp:** a brushed-metal base and cap, a glowing light leak at the collar, and a cord running off the table to the floor with an inline switch you can click.
- **Room:** a wood table, plaster walls, a moonlit window, books, a mug, a succulent, a brass ball and a framed print.
- **Panel:** power, six colour presets (including classic red wax in yellow liquid), heat, flow speed, wax amount, room light, slow motion and auto-orbit. All of them change the scene in real time.
- **Camera:** orbit is limited so the camera can't drop below the table or pass through the walls.
